newsitem.title: ISRAEL: Secrets of Dead Sea Scrolls unravel 50 years on.
newsitem.headline: Secrets of Dead Sea Scrolls unravel 50 years on.

text.p: Fifty years ago a shepherd searching the desert near Jerusalem for a stray goat stubbled upon a cave and uncovered one of the greatest finds of all time.

Now aided by technology, luck and the break-up of an academic dynasty, scholars are still unlocking the mysteries of the treasure -- complete documents and thousands of scraps known as the Dead Sea Scrolls.
Scholars cite the scrolls as both inspiring for Jewish continuity and a source of knowledge for Christian roots.

They also are learning more about the Essenes, the devout Jews who numbering 200 at the time and, living in isolation, wrote the manuscripts at a turning point in history 2,000 years ago when Judaism was in turmoil and Christianity was emerging.

"This was a time when people of this country tried to find the real truth for themselves. What was monotheism? What was faith? And therefore the importance of this period was so big until this day," archaeologist Avner Goren said on Sunday.
"The Dead Sea Scrolls shed a lot of light on their trying to find the right truth," Goren told reporters.

The Essenes -- who scorned as too lax their fellow Jews in the Jerusalem Temple establishment 40 kms (25 miles) away -- lived at Qumran beside the Dead Sea for 200 years until the Romans destroyed their settlement in 68 A.D.
"Whoever came here, came here to be alone," Goren said.

Faced with defeat, the sect hid its sacred works -- copies of the Hebrew Bible and Jewish writings along with codes and literature. They remained in the caves, some sealed in clay jars, until Bedouin shepherds and archaeologists uncovered them between 1947-56.

The Israel Museum in Jerusalem and Israel's Tourism Ministry organised a media tour of the site to launch a series of 50th anniversary exhibits and events expected to reach a climax in July when some 100 Dead Sea Scrolls world scholars meet in Jerusalem.

The international congress is a far cry from the scholarly monopoly and academic sniping that characterised the first 44 years after the scrolls' discovery when 80 percent of the material failed even to make it into print. Things changed in 1991 when the Israeli custodians of the scrolls abandoned efforts to limit access.

Visitors to Qumran can feel the coolness of the caves that dot the slopes and crevices and visit the remains of the stone complex where the Essenes had their ritual baths and ceremonial meals and wrote their texts.
Scholars say the arid climate at this, the lowest point on earth, helped to preserve the scrolls which range from nearly complete documents to thousands of tiny scraps.

Piecing them together has been a challenge but a new tool -- DNA testing -- has enabled scholars to match fragments, unlocking new secrets in the scrolls, some of which are on display at the Israel Museum's "Shrine of the Book".
"We have thousands of fragments. Now we can know if they came from the same scrolls," said Adolfo Roitman, the Shrine of the Book director.
New preservation treatments are also important if the scrolls are to survive into later generations when new technologies will help further unravel their secrets.
Using new computer software, experts in 1994 were able to read scrolls that in the past could not be deciphered.
"Each new word may shed light on the history and theology of Judaism and the origins of Christianity. Sometimes just one new sentence may be very important to the scholar," Roitman said.
Luck also plays a role. A limestone object was found in the 1950s at Qumran. Its purpose unclear, the object was kept in a vault until the 1990s when it was recognised as a sundial.
The sundial -- remarkable because the Essenes kept time in a different way than their Jewish brethren in Jerusalem -- will be put on public display for the first time in July.
